## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Analysis and Deep Learning on Geometric Data
  Code                    CSC_53431_EP
  Team and workload       Instructor: Maks Ovsjanikov (École Polytechnique, LIX — Geometric Data Analysis group) · 24 h · 2 ECTS · discrete differential geometry, shape operators, functional maps, then deep learning on surfaces: classification, correspondence, parameterization.
  Period                  M2 · period 1 (master's wiki)
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2} M2 program being finalized by the course instructors (the wiki indicates that the detailed M2 curriculum is still under development); course unit description confirmed by the wiki, SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer comfortable with GNNs and meshes who wants the geometric operators behind shape analysis (the Laplacian, functional maps).

**Empirical first**: we start from what fails in practice — a shape-matching accuracy that collapses (from about 82% to 51% in a typical lab run) as soon as the mesh is remeshed, a 3D network that ignores curvature — and only then name the tools that fix it: the spectrum, functional maps, networks on surfaces.

The module goes from discrete differential geometry to deep learning on surfaces, following the work of Maks Ovsjanikov's Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) group.

### What you will be able to do

-   Discretize the notions of differential geometry on meshes.
-   Compute and interpret the Laplace-Beltrami operator and the spectrum of a shape.
-   Build shape descriptors and distances that are comparable across surfaces.
-   Put shapes in correspondence through functional maps.
-   Parameterize and process surfaces to make them usable.
-   Train networks that operate directly on surfaces.
-   Understand Euclidean equivariance and its role in geometric learning.

### Official objectives and syllabus

**Official description** (master's wiki): the SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet of this course unit is not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty); the description confirmed below is that of the wiki, which specifies the volume (24 h), credits (2 ECTS) and instructor.

An introduction to advanced topics in the modern analysis of geometric data, centered on a) the mathematical foundations — discrete differential geometry, mapping, optimization — and b) deep learning for the state-of-the-art methods: a panorama of the foundations of shape analysis and processing, then a move to modern deep-learning-based techniques to solve problems such as shape classification, correspondence and parameterization.

### Where this course fits in the program

M2 module (period 1), 24 h for 2 ECTS, mandatory. Its prerequisite is the mandatory M1 P2 course [Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html), whose spectral graph Laplacian foreshadows the Laplace-Beltrami operator; chapter 0 reactivates spectrum, surfaces and vector calculus.

The M1 P1 elective [Digital Representation and Analysis of Shapes](../m1p1-shapes/index.html) meets part of chapters 1–4 at an introductory level. These notes stay self-contained, since many students did not take it; a *Seen in Shapes* note at the start of each of those chapters says what Shapes students can skim.

Downstream, it prepares [Graph Generative Models and Applications](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html) — where 3D molecules become graphs to be generated — and is one of the entry routes toward the research track of the master.

### Course outline

-   **Reminders: spectrum, surfaces, vector calculus** — the mathematics of the module, put back in hand on surface examples.
-   **Discrete differential geometry** — transposing curvatures and derivatives to the discrete world of meshes.
-   **The Laplace-Beltrami operator** — the central spectral operator of shape analysis.
-   **Shape descriptors and distances** — comparing surfaces through computable signatures.
-   **Functional maps** — putting shapes in correspondence by transporting functions.
-   **Parameterization and processing** — flattening and parameterizing surfaces to process them.
-   **Deep learning on surfaces** — defining and training networks directly on geometry.
-   **Euclidean equivariance** — building models that respect the symmetries of space.
-   **Applications and LLGA connections** — where geometry meets the other tracks of the master.
-   **Course research notes — Geometric Data Analysis (Ovsjanikov)** — the papers of the Geometric Data Analysis group, read with the tools of the module (self-study).
-   **Exercises** — spectral computations and correspondences to carry out on real meshes.
-   **References** — the foundational papers of geometric analysis and learning on shapes.

### How to study this module

-   Connect each new operator to its graph cousin: the Graph ML Laplacian is the best anchor point of the module.
-   Visualize: eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, heat kernels, and descriptors are understood as colors on a mesh.
-   Implement the descriptors on small meshes before moving on to full datasets.
-   Redo chapter 0 without hesitation: vector calculus and spectra are used in every chapter.
-   Read the foundational papers on functional maps after the corresponding chapter — the course provides a guided reading of them.
-   Look early at the applications of chapter 8 and the research notes of chapter 9: that is where internship and research topics take shape.

## 0. Reminders: spectrum, surfaces, vector calculus {#ch0}

Every later chapter rests on three pieces of mathematics: the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, the notion of a surface, and integration by parts on it. This chapter recalls them, with proofs, and sets up the Fourier analogy that the module follows.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3/M1 prerequisites mobilized
:::

-   **Differential calculus**: gradient, divergence, Laplacian in $\mathbb{R}^2$ ($\Delta f = \partial_{xx} f + \partial_{yy} f$); Green's formula;
-   **Symmetric diagonalization**: $L = U\Lambda U^\top$, orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions — already seen for the *graph* Laplacian (Graph ML module, ch. 0);
-   **Convolution & Fourier** (Signal Processing module, if taken; recalled at the end of this chapter): the Laplacian is the frequency operator; heat diffusion $\partial_t u = \Delta u$;
-   **GNN** (Graph ML module): a mesh *is* a graph — but a geometric one (3D positions, metric).
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Spectral (reminder with proof)]{.tag} If $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is symmetric, its eigenvalues are real and there exists an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors:
$$A = U \Lambda U^\top .$$
Moreover the Rayleigh quotient satisfies
$$R(x) = \frac{x^\top A\, x}{x^\top x}, \qquad \lambda_{\min} = \min_{x \ne 0} R(x), \quad \lambda_{\max} = \max_{x \ne 0} R(x).$$
:::

::: proof
Standard sketch. $R$ is continuous on the (compact) unit sphere, so it attains its maximum at some $u_1$, $\|u_1\| = 1$.

On the sphere, the critical points of $R$ satisfy $Au = R(u)\,u$ (set the gradient of $x^\top A x$ to zero under the constraint $x^\top x = 1$, Lagrange multipliers): $u_1$ is an eigenvector.

Iterate on the orthogonal complement of $u_1$, which is stable under $A$ by symmetry:
$$\langle Au_1, v\rangle = \lambda_1\langle u_1, v\rangle = 0 .$$
This yields the basis by recursion.

The characterization of $\lambda_{\min}$/$\lambda_{\max}$ follows from $R(x) = \sum_k \lambda_k c_k^2$ with $\sum_k c_k^2 = 1$ (barycenter of the $\lambda_k$). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: prop
[Generalized problem]{.tag} Geometric operators give pairs $(K, M)$: a symmetric positive semi-definite *stiffness* matrix $K$ and a positive definite *mass* matrix $M$ (ch. 1 builds both). One solves
$$K\phi = \lambda M\phi .$$
Setting $\tilde K = M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ (symmetric!), thm. 0.1 applies and $\phi = M^{-1/2}\tilde\phi$; the eigenvectors are $M$-orthonormal, $\phi_k^\top M \phi_l = \delta_{kl}$. This is the `eigsh(K, k, M=M, sigma=-1e-8)` call of the lab sessions (SciPy, shift-invert just below 0).
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Surface, charts, atlas]{.tag} A *surface* (2-dimensional manifold) is a set covered by **charts**: bijections $x : U \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to V \subset M$ whose chart transitions $x_2^{-1} \circ x_1$ are smooth. The collection of charts is an **atlas**.

*Example: the sphere.* Two stereographic charts (from the North pole and the South pole) suffice; on their intersection, the chart transition is the inversion $u \mapsto u/\|u\|^2$ — smooth.

A function $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth if $f \circ x$ is in every chart; intrinsic quantities (lengths, areas, Laplacian) do not depend on the chosen chart.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Vector calculus: Green's formula and self-adjointness]{.tag} Gradient (direction of steepest slope), divergence (outgoing flux per unit area), $\Delta f = \mathrm{div}\,\nabla f$.

Green's formula (geometric integration by parts),
$$\int_{\Omega} \langle \nabla f, \nabla g\rangle\, dA = -\int_\Omega f\,\Delta g\, dA + \oint_{\partial\Omega} f\,\partial_n g\, ds,$$
is *the* reason why the Laplacian is symmetric. On a *closed* surface (without boundary),
$$\int f \Delta g = \int g \Delta f$$
— and this symmetry carries over to the discrete setting (ch. 2).
:::

| Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$ | Surface $M$ |
|---|---|
| translations/rotations | isometries of $M$ |
| exponentials $e^{i\langle \omega, x\rangle}$ | eigenfunctions $\phi_k$ of $\Delta_M$ |
| frequencies $\|\omega\|^2$ | eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ |
| convolution (translation invariant) | operators that are functions of $\Delta_M$ |
| low-pass filter | attenuating the high $\lambda_k$ |

**Convolution and Fourier (reminder).** Convolution $(f * g)(x) = \int f(x-y)g(y)dy$ is the unique commutative, bilinear, continuous, translation-invariant product. The Fourier transform diagonalizes it:
$$\widehat{f*g} = \hat f \cdot \hat g, \qquad \widehat{\Delta f} = -\|\omega\|^2\hat f .$$
This whole machinery *disappears* on a surface (no translation group); the Laplacian — and it alone — plays its role: this is the program of chapters 2–4.

## 1. Discrete differential geometry {#ch1}

A computer stores a surface as a mesh of triangles, while curvature, gradients and the Laplacian are defined on smooth surfaces. This chapter transposes these notions to meshes. A concrete scene shows why they matter: to align two scans of the same object, raw XYZ coordinates work when the pose is fixed but break as soon as the object bends; we need *intrinsic* quantities, which do not change under such deformations.

::: note
[Seen in Shapes]{.tag} Students who took the M1 elective *Digital Representation and Analysis of Shapes* met the mixed Voronoi areas and the cotangent weights in [Shapes ch. 5](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch5), and the angle deficit with the discrete Gauss–Bonnet theorem in [Shapes ch. 7](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch7). For them, Construction 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 are revision to skim before session 2; the finite-element view at the end of the chapter is new.

Notation used from here on, the convention of [Shapes ch. 5](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch5): $K$ is the stiffness (cotangent) matrix, positive semi-definite, $M$ the mass (area) matrix, the discrete Laplacian is $L = -M^{-1}K$, and spectra solve $K\phi = \lambda M\phi$.
:::

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three classic failures: extrinsic features (coordinates, normals) that change when the shape bends without stretching; a badly discretized Laplacian on a non-manifold mesh; and too few eigenmodes to resolve the details one needs.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Triangulated surface]{.tag} A mesh $M = (V, E, F)$: vertices $v_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, edges, triangular faces. It is both a *graph* and an approximation of a smooth *surface*; the mixed Voronoi area $A_i$ associates a "zone" with each vertex.
:::

::: prop
[Construction 1.2 — Barycentric Voronoi areas (computation)]{.tag} Each vertex $i$ receives, within each incident triangle, the portion of the Voronoi cell contained in that triangle. Summed up, the dual area is written *per edge*:
$$A_i = \frac{1}{8}\sum_{j \sim i}\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big)\,\|v_i - v_j\|^2,$$
where $\alpha_{ij}, \beta_{ij}$ are the angles opposite to edge $(i,j)$.

*Check on a regular triangular lattice of side $a$*: each vertex has 6 neighbors, each edge has two opposite angles of $60°$, hence $\cot\alpha + \cot\beta = 2/\sqrt3$ per edge and
$$A_i = \frac{1}{8}\cdot 6\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\,a^2 = \frac{\sqrt3\,a^2}{2} = 6 \times \frac{A_T}{3}, \qquad A_T = \frac{\sqrt3\,a^2}{4},$$
that is, exactly one third of the area of each of the six incident triangles.

For *obtuse* triangles, the per-edge formula can become negative: one switches locally to the barycenter ("mixed", Meyer et al. 2003).
:::

::: thm
[Discrete curvature: the Gauss angle deficit]{.tag}
$$K_i = \frac{2\pi - \sum_{f \ni i}\theta_{i,f}}{A_i}$$
(flat ⇒ $K = 0$; cone ⇒ positive; saddle ⇒ negative). This is a *total measure* of Gaussian curvature over the zone $A_i$.
:::

::: proof
Why $2\pi$ minus the sum of the angles? Transport a tangent vector *parallel to itself* around vertex $i$, staying on the faces. Unfold the incident faces one after the other into the plane, so that inside each face and across each edge the vector does not rotate (the faces are flat).

The unfolded faces cover a total angle $\sum_f \theta_{i,f}$ instead of $2\pi$. So when the loop closes, the final vector makes with the initial one an angle equal to the *deficit*:
$$2\pi - \sum_f \theta_{i,f} .$$

Now on a smooth surface, parallel transport around a loop encircling a total Gaussian curvature $\int K\,dA$ rotates by exactly this angle (local Gauss–Bonnet theorem, "transport" equivalent of the *theorema egregium*: curvature is intrinsic). The deficit is therefore the discrete analogue of $\int_{A_i} K\,dA$, hence the density $K_i$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Discrete Gauss–Bonnet (statement + numerical example)]{.tag}
$$\sum_{i \in V} K_i\, A_i \;=\; \sum_i \Big(2\pi - \sum_{f\ni i}\theta_{i,f}\Big) \;=\; 2\pi\,\chi(M), \qquad \chi = |V| - |E| + |F|.$$
The total curvature depends only on the *topology*.

*Example: the cube.* Eight vertices, three squares (faces split into triangles: angles of $\pi/2$) meet at each vertex. The deficit per vertex and the total are
$$2\pi - 3\times\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad 8 \times \frac{\pi}{2} = 4\pi = 2\pi \times 2$$
— the characteristic of the sphere.

*A useful counterexample*: the torus (donut) has $\chi = 0$: however it is meshed, the positive and negative deficits cancel out exactly.
:::

::: prop
[Principal curvatures, mean curvature: via the Laplacian of positions]{.tag} At each point, the normal sections of the surface have extreme curvatures $k_1 \le k_2$ (*principal*); Gaussian curvature $K = k_1k_2$ (the deficit approximates it); mean curvature $H = \frac{k_1+k_2}{2}$.

*Vector* version, computable directly on the mesh:
$$\Delta_M\, \mathbf{x} = 2H\,\mathbf{n} \qquad\text{(positions }\mathbf{x}(p) \text{ viewed as 3 functions on } M\text{)}.$$

*Justification (sketch).* The vector $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ is the gradient of area: varying the surface by $\varepsilon\,f\,\mathbf{n}$ changes the area by $\varepsilon \int 2Hf\,dA$ (first variation; minimal surfaces — soap bubbles — are those with $H = 0$). Now computing the gradient of area by integration by parts (prop. 0.3) brings out $\Delta\mathbf{x}$; normalizing by the normal yields the formula.

In the discrete setting,
$$\mathbf{H}_i = \frac12 (L\mathbf{x})_i$$
with the cotangent Laplacian of ch. 2 — one line of libigl.
:::

-   **Normal of a face**: $n_f \propto (v_j - v_i) \times (v_k - v_i)$; vertex normal: area-weighted (or angle-weighted) average;
-   **Barycentric coordinates**: in a triangle $(i,j,k)$, every point can be written $\alpha v_i + \beta v_j + \gamma v_k$, $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$, with $\alpha$ = normalized area of the opposite sub-triangle; they serve to *interpolate* any function from the vertices to the interior of the faces (a mesh carries values only at vertices);
-   **Finite differences vs finite elements**: the "FD" route approximates $\Delta f$ by combinations of neighbors (like the graph Laplacian). The "FEM" route projects onto the basis of **hat functions** $\psi_i$ (1 at $v_i$, 0 at the other vertices, affine on the faces) and assembles the **stiffness matrix**
    $$K_{ij} = \int_M \langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle\, dA, \qquad M_{ij} = \int_M \psi_i\psi_j\, dA\ \ (\text{mass}),$$
    giving the operator $L = -M^{-1}K$; with the mass lumped onto the diagonal, $M = \mathrm{diag}(A_i)$, it is the cotangent matrix of ch. 2, and $-L$ is positive semi-definite. The explicit computation of $K_{ij}$ on a triangle — an object of ch. 2 — recovers *exactly* the cotangents: FEM and discrete geometry converge. (The stiffness matrix $K$ carries two indices; the Gaussian curvature $K_i$ above carries one.)

::: note
[Useful jargon]{.tag} The pair $(K, M)$ of ch. 0 is called "stiffness/mass" here; the convergence of discrete operators toward the smooth Laplace-Beltrami (as the mesh is refined) is subtle — the cotangent one converges in the weak sense (Wardetzky 2007); this is *the* reason why DiffusionNet (ch. 6, ch. 9) prefers to require only *heat operators* from the discrete setting.
:::

## 2. The Laplace-Beltrami operator {#ch2}

On a surface there is no Fourier transform, because there are no translations; the operator that takes its place is the Laplacian of the surface. This chapter builds it on meshes (the cotangent matrix), derives it from an energy, and proves the two properties that make it the central tool of shape analysis: its eigenfunctions act as frequencies, and it does not change when the surface bends without stretching.

::: note
[Seen in Shapes]{.tag} [Shapes ch. 5](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch5) used the cotangent Laplacian for smoothing, and [Shapes ch. 8](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch8) its spectrum and heat kernel. Shapes students can skim Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.3. Derivation 2.2 (the cotangents from the Dirichlet energy), the diffusion distances and the proof of isometric invariance (Theorem 2.5) are new.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Laplace-Beltrami]{.tag} The Laplacian *on the surface*:
$$\Delta_M f = \mathrm{div}_M(\nabla_M f).$$
In a local chart with metric $g = (g_{ab})$ (the $g_{ab}$ measure how the chart distorts lengths):
$$\Delta_M f = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}}\sum_{a,b}\partial_a\!\Big(\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{ab}\,\partial_b f\Big),$$
with $|g| = \det(g_{ab})$ and $(g^{ab})$ the inverse matrix, which recovers $\partial_{xx} + \partial_{yy}$ when $g = I$.

In the discrete setting, the **cotangent matrix**:
$$L_{ij} = \begin{cases} -\frac{1}{2A_i}\sum_{j \sim i}(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}) & i = j\\[2pt] \frac{1}{2A_i}(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}) & j \sim i\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
where $\alpha_{ij}, \beta_{ij}$ are the angles opposite to edge $(i,j)$.

In matrix form $L = -M^{-1}K$ (ch. 1), with $M = \mathrm{diag}(A_i)$, $K_{ij} = -w_{ij}$ for $j \sim i$ and $K_{ii} = \sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij}$, where $w_{ij}$ are the cotangent weights of Derivation 2.2 below.

Like the graph Laplacian (up to the sign convention), it is symmetric (in the $M$-self-adjoint sense), with $-L$ positive semi-definite. Its Fourier basis $\{\phi_k\}$ satisfies $\Delta \phi_k = -\lambda_k \phi_k$, with increasing $\lambda_k$ (= the "frequencies" of the surface).
:::

::: thm
[Derivation 2.2 — The cotangent operator via the Dirichlet energy]{.tag} The starting point is the Dirichlet energy (the "stiffness" of $f$):
$$E_D(f) = \tfrac12 \int_M \|\nabla f\|^2\, dA = \tfrac12\sum_{T}\int_T \|\nabla f\|^2\, dA.$$
By approximating $f$ with its barycentric interpolant (affine on each triangle, values $f_i$ at vertices), one gets an exact quadratic form:
$$E_D(f) = \tfrac14 \sum_{i}\sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij}\,(f_i - f_j)^2, \qquad w_{ij} = \tfrac12\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big)$$
(each edge is counted twice, once from each endpoint).

The cotangent matrix is the matrix of this quadratic form, normalized by the areas:
$$\frac{\partial E_D}{\partial f_i} = \sum_{j\sim i} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j) = -A_i\,(Lf)_i .$$
In words, $-A_i (Lf)_i$ is the gradient of the Dirichlet energy, and $Lf = 0$ characterizes the functions of minimal energy (harmonic functions).
:::

::: proof
**Step 1 — gradient of an affine function on a triangle.** On triangle $T = (i,j,k)$, the interpolant is
$$f = f_i\psi_i + f_j\psi_j + f_k\psi_k .$$
Each $\nabla\psi$ is *constant* on $T$, orthogonal to the opposite side, with norm $1/h$ (associated height). In particular
$$\nabla\psi_i + \nabla\psi_j + \nabla\psi_k = 0 .$$

**Step 2 — inner product of two gradients.** Let $h_i, h_j$ denote the heights from $i$ and $j$, and $\theta_k$ the angle at vertex $k$ (opposite to edge $(i,j)$).

The gradient $\nabla\psi_i$ is orthogonal to side $(j,k)$, points toward $i$, and $\|\nabla\psi_i\| = 1/h_i$; likewise $\|\nabla\psi_j\| = 1/h_j$, orthogonal to side $(i,k)$.

The two sides $(j,k)$ and $(i,k)$ making an angle $\theta_k$ with each other, their normals make an angle $\pi - \theta_k$, and the pointing directions flip the sign:
$$\langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle = -\frac{\cos\theta_k}{h_i h_j} \qquad \text{(constant on } T\text{)}.$$
Then, with $|T|$ the area and $|e|$ the side lengths:
$$\int_T \langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle\, dA = |T|\cdot\Big(-\frac{\cos\theta_k}{h_i h_j}\Big) = -\frac{|T|\,|e_{jk}|\,|e_{ik}|}{(2|T|)(2|T|)}\cos\theta_k = -\frac{\cos\theta_k}{2\sin\theta_k} = -\frac12\cot\theta_k,$$
where we used $h_i = 2|T|/|e_{jk}|$, $h_j = 2|T|/|e_{ik}|$ and then $|T| = \tfrac12|e_{jk}|\,|e_{ik}|\sin\theta_k$.

**Step 3 — assembly.** Each edge $(i,j)$ belongs to one or two triangles. Sum over these triangles the terms
$$\tfrac12 f_i f_j \int_T\langle\nabla\psi_i,\nabla\psi_j\rangle$$
and reorganize the quadratic form as $\tfrac14\sum_{ij} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)^2$ (the diagonal terms absorb the off-diagonal ones — exercise 6). The cotangent weights appear, with the contribution $-\tfrac12\cot\theta_k$ of each opposite triangle. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: key
[Key result — the cotangent weights]{.tag}
$$w_{ij} = \tfrac12\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big), \qquad -A_i\,(Lf)_i = \sum_{j\sim i} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)$$
:::

::: prop
[Properties (and why they hold)]{.tag}

-   **Symmetry**: $W = (w_{ij})$ is symmetric (each edge carries its weight, constructed symmetrically); this is the discrete version of the self-adjointness of ch. 0;
-   **Constants annihilated**: $L\mathbf{1} = 0$ because the quadratic form only sees the differences $f_i - f_j$;
-   **Positivity**: $E_D(f) \ge 0$, zero iff $f$ is constant (on each connected component); hence $\lambda_1 = 0$ has multiplicity 1 and $\lambda_2 > 0$ measures the "connectivity" (the Fiedler value of surfaces);
-   **Convergence**: as the mesh is refined, $L$ converges to $\Delta_M$ in the weak sense — subject to triangle quality (no too-obtuse angles; Wardetzky 2007);
-   **Nodal sets**: the zeros of $\phi_k$ cut the surface into increasingly fine regions as $k$ grows — the "wavefronts" of the surface; $\lambda_k \sim c\,k$ (Weyl's law in dimension 2).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Heat kernel: spectral construction]{.tag} The solution of the heat equation $\partial_t u = \Delta u$, $u(0) = u_0$, reads (recall $\Delta\phi_k = -\lambda_k\phi_k$ with $\lambda_k \ge 0$)
$$u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\langle \phi_k, u_0\rangle\,\phi_k, \qquad h_t(x, y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y).$$
Each mode $\phi_k$ is damped by $e^{-\lambda_k t}$: diffusion = spectral low-pass filtering.
:::

::: proof
Direct substitution, term by term (using $\Delta\phi_k = -\lambda_k\phi_k$):
$$\partial_t\big[e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k\big] = -\lambda_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k = \Delta\big[e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k\big].$$
At $t = 0$, the sum reduces to $\sum_k\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k = u_0$ (orthonormal basis — for the $M$-weighted inner product of the lab sessions).

The kernel $h_t$ is just the same writing in "integral" form: $u(x,t) = \int h_t(x,y)u_0(y)dy$ (exercise 4). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Diffusion distances: geometry of the heat kernel]{.tag}
$$D_t^2(x, y) = \|h_t(x, \cdot) - h_t(y, \cdot)\|^2_{L^2} = \sum_k e^{-2\lambda_k t}\,\big(\phi_k(x) - \phi_k(y)\big)^2.$$
Two points are close if their "thermal fingerprints" are close; the exponential weighting short-circuits high frequencies — robust to noise, unlike the geodesic distance. This is the building block of the diffusion geometry of ch. 3.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — Isometric invariance (proved)]{.tag} If $T : M \to N$ is an isometry (preserves the lengths of curves), then for every $f$ on $N$ and every $x \in M$:
$$\Delta_M (f \circ T)(x) = (\Delta_N f)(T(x)).$$
Consequence: identical spectra, transported eigenfunctions — the foundation of all non-rigid shape comparison.
:::

::: proof
An isometry preserves lengths and areas, hence inner products of gradients and integration: for all $u, v$ on $N$,
$$\int_N \langle\nabla u, \nabla v\rangle\, dA_N = \int_M \langle\nabla(u\circ T), \nabla(v\circ T)\rangle\, dA_M$$
(change of variable $T$, Jacobian = 1).

By Green's formula (prop. 0.3 — self-adjointness), for every $v$,
$$\int v\,\Delta_N u = \int (v\circ T)\,\Delta_M(u\circ T).$$
Since this holds for every test function $v\circ T$ (surjective), $\Delta_M(u\circ T) = (\Delta_N u)\circ T$ pointwise. [∎]{.qed}
:::

```python
import igl                     # libigl: reference discrete geometry library
import numpy as np

import scipy.sparse.linalg as sla

v, f = igl.read_triangle_mesh("bunny.obj")
K = -igl.cotmatrix(v, f)                    # stiffness K (libigl's cotmatrix is negative semi-definite)
M = igl.massmatrix(v, f, igl.MASSMATRIX_TYPE_VORONOI)   # lumped mass diag(A_i)
# generalized problem K phi = lambda M phi (ch. 0): the 20 smallest eigenpairs
evals, evecs = sla.eigsh(K, k=20, M=M, sigma=-1e-8)
# visualize evecs[:, k] as a "texture" on the mesh -> vibration modes
# NB: the heat operator never requires L explicitly:
B = igl.grad(v, f)                          # per-face gradients (3|F| x |V|)
# E_D(f) = 0.5 * f^T K f = 0.5 * sum over faces of area * |grad f|^2
```

::: note
[Why this is the central tool]{.tag}

-   **Isometric invariance**: the spectrum does not change if the surface is "bent" without stretching — *non-rigid* shape comparison (a moving human);
-   **Diffusion**: heat $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0$ — "Can one hear the shape of a drum?": the spectrum encodes the geometry (with honest limits, ch. 3);
-   **Reduced dimension**: projecting onto the first $k$ eigenfunctions ≈ PCA of the surface; all of ch. 4 follows from it.
:::

## 3. Shape descriptors and distances {#ch3}

To compare or match two shapes we need, at each point, a signature that is computable and unchanged when the shape bends. This chapter builds such descriptors from the spectrum of chapter 2 (HKS, WKS, ShapeDNA), together with intrinsic distances, and states the limit of the whole spectral approach.

::: note
[Seen in Shapes]{.tag} [Shapes ch. 8](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch8) introduced ShapeDNA, the heat-kernel and wave-kernel signatures and the isospectral counterexample. Shapes students can skim Definition 3.1 and the list of descriptors; the stability proof of the HKS and the scale normalization are new.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Heat Kernel Signature (HKS)]{.tag} The amount of residual heat at $x$ after time $t$:
$$\mathrm{HKS}(x, t) = h_t(x, x) = \sum_k e^{-t\lambda_k}\, \phi_k(x)^2$$
— an *intrinsic* descriptor: stable, isometrically invariant; multi-scale (small $t$ = local detail, large = global). These signatures play the role of "features" for correspondence.
:::

::: proof
**Stability (proved sketch).** Perturb the metric by $\|\delta g\| \le \varepsilon$ (scan noise, different mesh). The perturbations of the eigenvalues (Weyl's theorem) and of the eigenfunctions are bounded by
$$|\delta\lambda_k| \le C\varepsilon\lambda_k, \qquad \|\delta\phi_k\| \le C'\varepsilon\lambda_k/\mathrm{gap}_k,$$
where $\mathrm{gap}_k$ is the local spectral gap — this is why one avoids multiple eigenvalues. Then
$$|\delta\mathrm{HKS}(x,t)| \le \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\big(|\delta\lambda_k|\,t\,\phi_k(x)^2 + 2\|\phi_k\|\|\delta\phi_k\|\big) = O(\varepsilon)\,\sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\lambda_k\phi_k(x)^2,$$
a convergent series for every $t > 0$ (Weyl-type growth against exponential decay): the HKS is Lipschitz in the metric — *hence its empirical robustness*.

Note that this computation also justifies the limitation: at large $t$, only the small $\lambda_k$ contribute (a global, not very discriminative descriptor); at small $t$, the series is sensitive to high frequencies (noise); hence the choice of a *logarithmic* grid of $t$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

-   **Scale-normalized HKS**: dividing $\mathrm{HKS}(x, t)$ by its max at $x$ (or by $\max_x\mathrm{HKS}(x,t)$) makes the descriptor *scale-invariant* — the $\lambda_k$ rescale by $s^{-2}$ when the shape is dilated by $s$, and the normalization absorbs the factor;
-   **Wave Kernel Signature** (Aubry et al., 2011): a quantum particle of energy $e$ distributed log-uniformly:
    $$\mathrm{WKS}(x, e) = \sum_k \phi_k(x)^2 e^{-(\log e - \log\lambda_k)^2/2\sigma^2}$$
    — a Gaussian window *on a logarithmic scale*: each energy probes one precise frequency band (better localization than the HKS, whose every $t$ mixes low frequencies);
-   **ShapeDNA** (Reuter et al.): the vector $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ — normalized by area — as a global "fingerprint"; $L^2$ distance between fingerprints;
-   **Intrinsic distances**:

    -   *geodesic* (shortest path on the surface): Dijkstra's algorithm on the graph of the mesh (edge lengths) = lower bound;
    -   continuous refinement (Fast Marching, Kimmel–Sethian) solves the eikonal equation $\|\nabla d\| = 1$ by a growing wavefront;
    -   the modern "heat method" variant (Crane et al.) first solves heat and then takes its renormalized gradient — O(linear solver);
    -   *diffusion distance* (prop. 2.4): truncated spectral approximations of both;

-   **Can one hear the shape of a drum?** No — Gordon, Webb, and Wolpert (1992) constructed pairs of surfaces that are *isospectral but not isometric*. The spectrum does not determine the shape: this is a fundamental (and mathematically sound) limit of the whole spectral pipeline — ShapeDNA, spectral constraints of functional maps, HKS.

    In practice: the spectrum discriminates *almost everything*, and one always complements it with operator and descriptor constraints (ch. 4);
-   **Flattening (embedding)**: the first $k$ eigenfunctions give an embedding $x \mapsto (\phi_1(x), \dots, \phi_k(x))$ that "unfolds" the shape — the exact analogue of spectral clustering for graphs ([Graph ML ch. 4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch4)) and of the Laplacian positional encodings of Advanced GNN ch. 4 (an announced M2 P1 module): same algebra, different object.

## 4. Functional maps {#ch4}

Finding which point of one shape corresponds to which point of another is a huge combinatorial problem. This chapter replaces it with a small linear one: instead of matching points, we transport functions, and in the spectral bases of chapter 2 the map becomes a $k \times k$ matrix.

::: note
[Seen in Shapes]{.tag} Shapes Definition 8.4 ([Shapes ch. 8](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch8)) described functional maps in one paragraph. This chapter develops them in full: constraints, proofs, resolution and refinement.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem/Concept 4.1 — Functional Maps (Ovsjanikov et al., 2012)]{.tag} Instead of looking for the point-to-point correspondence (a combinatorial discrete map, costly), transport *functions* defined on the surfaces:
$$T_F : \mathcal{F}(M) \to \mathcal{F}(N), \qquad T_F(g) = g \circ T^{-1}$$
Restricted to the spectral bases $\Phi_M, \Phi_N$ (the first $k$ eigenfunctions), the map becomes a **small matrix $C \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$**:
$$b_N \approx C\, b_M \quad (b = \Phi^\top f).$$
A correspondence of $10^5$ points is replaced by $k^2$ numbers ($k \sim 30$): this is the paradigm shift of the field.
:::

::: key
[Key result — a map between shapes is a small matrix]{.tag}
$$b_N \approx C\, b_M, \qquad C \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}, \quad b = \Phi^\top f$$
:::

::: prop
[Constraints 4.2 — what C must satisfy]{.tag}

-   **Descriptor preservation**: if $D_M \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times q}$ are the coefficients of $q$ descriptors (HKS, WKS...) on $M$ and $D_N$ on $N$ (in the same order):
    $$C\,D_M \approx D_N \qquad (k \times q \text{ equations});$$
-   **Commutation with operators**:
    $$C\,\Lambda_M \approx \Lambda_N\,C$$
    (spectral regularization — the subject of the proof below);
-   **Orthogonality**: if one believes in an isometry, $C^\top C \approx I$ (preserves inner products of functions; follows from $\Phi_N^\top C = \Phi_M^\top$ for orthonormal bases);
-   **Correspondence coupling**: if a few pairs of points are known, $\Phi_N^\top \Pi^\top \Phi_M \approx C$ with $\Pi$ the permutation matrix (*hard* constraint vs least squares).
:::

::: proof
**Commutation: proved.** Assume $T : M \to N$ is an isometry and let $T_F$ denote the transport of functions. The invariance theorem of ch. 2 (Theorem 2.5) says: $\Delta_M(f \circ T) = (\Delta_N f)\circ T$, in other words
$$\Delta_M \, T_F = T_F\, \Delta_N \quad\text{(after identifying the directions)}.$$

Apply to $f = \phi_k^N$ (eigenfunction of $N$, $\Delta_N\phi_k^N = -\lambda_k^N\phi_k^N$):
$$\Delta_M\,T_F\phi_k^N = T_F(-\lambda_k^N\phi_k^N) = -\lambda_k^N\,T_F\phi_k^N .$$
*The transport of an eigenfunction is an eigenfunction for the same eigenvalue*.

If the spectrum is simple, $T_F\phi_k^N = \pm\phi_k^M$. In the eigenbasis, the matrix of $T_F$ is therefore *almost diagonal*: $C_{ij} \ne 0$ only if $\lambda_i^M$ and $\lambda_j^N$ coincide — hence the constraint $C\Lambda_M \approx \Lambda_N C$ (weak: in the least-squares sense, since real surfaces are only approximately isometric and multiple eigenvalues create blocks). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Resolution 4.3 — least squares and normal equations]{.tag}
$$C^* = \arg\min_C\ \big\|C D_M - D_N\big\|_F^2 + \alpha\big\|C\Lambda_M - \Lambda_N C\big\|_F^2 + \beta\big\|C^\top C - I\big\|_F^2 + \mu\|C\|_F^2.$$
Without the orthogonality term, each *row* $c_i$ of $C$ is solved independently by normal equations:
$$c_i = \big(D_M D_M^\top + \alpha\,\Omega + \mu I\big)^{-1} D_M d_i^{\;N\top},$$
with $\Omega$ the regularization matrix derived from commutation — a $k \times k$ linear system solved in a few milliseconds.

With orthogonality, one projects onto rotations (SVD: $C \leftarrow UV^\top$ — Procrustes projection).
:::

::: prop
[Conversion to point-to-point correspondence + refinement]{.tag} **Soft correspondence**:
$$P = \Phi_N\, C\, \Phi_M^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{|V_N| \times |V_M|}, \qquad \Pi(x) = \arg\max_y P_{yx}$$
— the matrix $P$ (barely dense, a product of three long matrices) encodes the "probability" that $y$ corresponds to $x$.

**Refinement (the ZoomOut spirit, ch. 9)**: iteratively,

1.  increase $k$ by one notch;
2.  recompute $C$ using the current hard correspondence as a coupling constraint;
3.  re-derive $P$.

The growing spectral resolution acts as *annealing*: large structures settle at small $k$ (strong regularization), details adjust afterwards — algorithm:

```python
C = least_squares(k=k0, descriptors)          # coarse start
for k in range(k0, kmax, step):
    Pi = argmax_per_column(Phi_N[k] @ C @ Phi_M[k].T)   # hard
    C = solve(constraints + coupling(Pi), dim=k)        # soft
return Pi                                          # final correspondence
```
:::

-   **Partial maps**: when only a *part* of $M$ corresponds to $N$, $T_F$ becomes a restriction; the matrix $C$ is then *rectangular* (or one embeds $M$ into $N$ via a prolongation operator); the constraints adapt (descriptors only on the visible part);
-   **Learned extensions**: the descriptors $D$ can be produced by a network (SpectralNet, then *GeomFMaps* — deep geometric functional maps): the network learns descriptors that are *optimal for the matrix C*, the resolution remaining a differentiable least squares; the complete computation graph (network → C → correspondence loss) is trained end to end;
-   **Supervised vs unsupervised**: with annotated pairs (FAUST), one directly supervises the geodesic error of $\Pi$; otherwise, one maximizes orthogonality and preservation (HKS on both sides): unsupervised works well for quasi-isometries (humans);
-   **Applications**: *texture transfer*: the texture (a color function!) on $M$ is transported by $b_N = C\,b_M$ — a matrix multiplication; pose transfer (the correspondence coordinates), morphing;
-   **LLGA connection**: a functional map ≈ an *optimal transport* between reduced bases; shape alignment ≈ graph alignment by Gromov-Wasserstein (OT module, ch. 5); the three languages — GNN, OT, functional maps — describe the same operation of *structural correspondence*.

## 5. Parameterization and processing {#ch5}

Many tasks — texturing, remeshing, editing, reconstruction from a scan — need a surface to be flattened, smoothed or rebuilt. This chapter shows that most of these operations reduce to minimizing an energy built on the Laplacian of chapter 2, hence to solving a sparse linear system.

::: thm
[Harmonic maps — equations proved]{.tag} Flatten a surface with boundary onto the disk $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$: look for $u : M \to \mathbb{R}^2$ minimizing the Dirichlet energy $E_D(u) = \tfrac12\int\|\nabla u\|^2$ with the boundary fixed on $\partial\Omega$ (unit circle, uniformly — *Tutte*).
:::

::: proof
First variation: for every perturbation $\delta u$ that vanishes on the boundary,
$$0 = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}E_D(u + \varepsilon\,\delta u)\Big|_{\varepsilon=0} = \int_M \langle\nabla u, \nabla\delta u\rangle\, dA = -\int_M \delta u\,\Delta u\, dA + \oint_{\partial M}\delta u\,\partial_n u\, ds.$$
The boundary term vanishes ($\delta u = 0$ on $\partial M$). Since $\delta u$ is arbitrary *in the interior*, the minimizer is **harmonic** (component by component):
$$\Delta u \equiv 0 .$$

Tutte's theorem further guarantees that if the boundary is sent to the *convex* contour of the circle, the map is injective (no folding).

In the discrete setting: the discrete Dirichlet energy (derivation 2.2!) leads to the linear system $L u = 0$ with boundary rows replaced by the constraints — a Poisson solver, a few tens of milliseconds. [∎]{.qed}
:::

-   **Conformal**: a map is conformal if it preserves *angles* — the local Jacobian is a similarity $du = s\,R$ (Cauchy–Riemann intuition: real and imaginary parts are *conjugate* harmonic); it preserves the shape of small details (textures without shear), but distorts areas; the algorithms (LSCM and descendants) enforce conformity through quadratic constraints;
-   **ARAP — as-rigid-as-possible**: minimize
    $$E_{\mathrm{ARAP}}(u) = \sum_{T}\min_{R_T \in SO(2)} \big\|J_T(u) - R_T\big\|_F^2,$$
    where $J_T(u)$ is the Jacobian of the map on face $T$ and $R_T$ the "closest" rotation. *Local/global* solver:

    a.  local: each face fixes $R_T = UV^\top$ (SVD of $J_T$);
    b.  global: with the rotations fixed, $E$ becomes quadratic in $u$ → linear system;

    alternate until convergence — a geometric EM; an angle/area compromise without excessive distortion;
-   **Spectral smoothing/filtering**: attenuate high frequencies (denoise), sharpening — signal processing (M1) transported to surfaces;
-   **Deformation: laplacian editing**: move handles while preserving $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ of the positions (the details): minimize $\sum\|L\mathbf{x}' - L\mathbf{x}\|^2$ under constraints — the same machinery as the harmonic map; skinning, morphing — graphics/AR applications of the sister ViCAI module;
-   **Poisson reconstruction**: from a normal field $\mathbf{v}$ (oriented, scan): look for the surface $\chi$ (indicator function) such that
    $$\nabla\chi = \mathbf{v} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Delta\chi = \mathrm{div}\,\mathbf{v}$$
    (projection of the field onto gradients — in the least-squares sense, then a Poisson solve); this is the bridge scan → closed mesh;
-   **Decimation — quadric error metric**: associate to each vertex the quadric (sum of the products of the unit plane equations)
    $$Q_i = \sum_{p \in \text{incident planes}} A_p^\top A_p .$$
    The cost of contracting edge $(i,j)$ to the point $\bar v$ is $Q_{ij}(\bar v) = Q_i(\bar v) + Q_j(\bar v)$ — a quadratic form, minimized in closed form; one contracts the lowest-cost edges with a binary heap;
-   **Curvature-based remeshing**: vertex density $\propto$ local curvature (deficit of ch. 1) — allocate the triangle budget where the geometry demands it.

```python
# Spectral smoothing: low-pass filtering on the eigenfunctions
import numpy as np
# evals, evecs: outputs of igl.eigs (ch. 2); f: per-vertex function
k = 30
coef = evecs.T @ (M_diag * f)              # spectral coefficients
coef[:, k:] = 0                            # cut the high frequencies
f_smooth = evecs @ coef
# soft variant: coef *= 1/(1 + (evals/lambda0)**2)  (Butterworth)
```

## 6. Deep learning on surfaces {#ch6}

The networks of image processing assume a regular grid, which point clouds and meshes do not have. This chapter presents the architectures that learn directly on 3D data — PointNet and its local extensions, then DiffusionNet — and the obstacle they all face: a surface has no canonical orientation for a filter.

::: thm
[Architecture 6.1 — PointNet (Qi et al., 2017)]{.tag} Point clouds (without a mesh): per point: shared MLP; global **max** aggregation (permutation-invariant — the same requirement as GNNs, Graph ML module ch. 2); cloud classification/segmentation:
$$f(X) = \rho\Big(\max_{x_i \in X}\ \gamma(x_i)\Big), \qquad |X| = n,\ x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3.$$
:::

::: proof
**Invariance.** A permutation $\pi$ reorders the rows of $X$; the entrywise max of a set does not depend on the order (the shared MLP is applied column by column):
$$f(\pi X) = f(X).$$

*Why max rather than another invariant aggregator?*

-   The product $\prod_i \gamma(x_i)$ is likewise permutation-invariant, but numerically disastrous (explodes toward 0 or $\infty$, unstable multiplicative gradients);
-   the mean is stable but *dilutes* local signals — a discriminative sub-region representing 1% of the cloud is drowned;
-   the max is *selective*: it captures "at least one point exhibits the characteristic", which is exactly the building block of the universal approximation that follows.

**Universality (sketch).** On a compact set $K$, a continuous permutation-invariant function can be uniformly approximated by sums of "soft indicator functions" of balls:
$$g(x) \approx \sum_j c_j\,\mathbb{1}_{B(c_j, r_j)}(x).$$
Now, with $h_\varepsilon$ a steep sigmoid,
$$\mathbb{1}_{B(c,r)}(x) \approx h_\varepsilon(\|x - c\|),$$
and
$$\max_{x_i}\big[1 - h_\varepsilon(\|x_i - c\|)\big]$$
equals \~1 as soon as *a single* point falls in the ball. The union of balls is expressed via the max: PointNet approximates the functions of "membership of at least one point in a ball", the universal building block for compact sets (thm. 1 of the paper). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[PointNet++ and DGCNN — injecting the local]{.tag} PointNet only sees *unions* of regions (the global max ignores co-localization). Two answers:

-   **PointNet++**:

    a.  *farthest point sampling*: iteratively choose the point farthest from the already chosen centers (uniform coverage, greedy algorithm in $O(n\,k)$);
    b.  *ball query*: group the neighbors in a ball of fixed radius;
    c.  a *local* PointNet per group, then a hierarchy (progressive subsampling — exactly a spatial pooling);

    multi-scale through nested radii;

-   **DGCNN**: *dynamic* k-NN graph in feature space (EdgeConv):
    $$x_i' = \square_{j : (i,j) \in \mathrm{kNN}}\ h_\theta(x_i, x_j), \qquad h_\theta(x_i, x_j) = \mathrm{MLP}\big(x_i,\ x_j - x_i\big),$$
    the max (or mean) over the edges; the graph is rebuilt at every layer — the neighbors drift apart in latent space: a growing receptive field (from local to global, like stacked convolutions).
:::

::: prop
[Geodesic convolutions and the gauge problem]{.tag} A convolution filters a *patch* (geodesic neighborhood, anisotropic). But on a surface, **there is no canonical frame** in the tangent plane: where should "north" go? Every choice of gauge (local rotation of the frame) rotates the filter: an anisotropic filter is not *well-defined*. Three strategies:

-   measure the alignment with an extrinsic direction (the gradient, the normal) — fragile;
-   principal coordinates (eigenframes of the curvature tensor): stable but sign-ambiguous;
-   isotropic filtering (angularly invariant): one gives up anisotropy — this is the spectral answer (filters that are functions of $\Delta$, cf. ChebNet of the Graph ML module) and... the DiffusionNet answer below.
:::

::: thm
[DiffusionNet (Sharp, Attaiki, Crane, Ovsjanikov — TOG 2022): complete equations]{.tag} Replace convolution with **learned diffusion**. Each layer transforms features $H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$:

1.  **Learned diffusion**: learn $m$ scales $t_1, \dots, t_m > 0$ (free parameters):
    $$H \leftarrow \mathrm{concat}\Big(H,\ \ \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j\, e^{t_j\Delta}H\Big) \ \ \text{(learned mixture of heats at all scales)};$$
2.  **Per-point MLP**: $H \leftarrow \mathrm{MLP}(H)$ — a *pointwise* operator (no gauge!);
3.  **Gradient of features**: the gradient $\nabla_M H$ (tangent vector per vertex, cotangent-Derivation 2.2 generalized) contains the *direction* of the variations — anisotropy reintroduced *without* a frame: concatenated to $H$;
4.  back to (1) — 8–12 layers.

**Properties**: discretization-agnostic (only the heat operators $e^{t\Delta}$ and $\nabla$ are required — available on meshes *and* point clouds via heat estimation); isotropic (no gauge) + directional gradient; learned scales (no more fixed grid of $t$); SOTA on FAUST/SCAPE at the time, robust to re-meshings — the "discrete element" of the field.
:::

-   **Transformers on surfaces**: global attention between points/vertices with *intrinsic* positional encodings (HKS, random geodesic distances) as the positional add-on: the GPS recipe (global attention + local message passing; Advanced GNN ch. 5, an announced M2 P1 module) transplanted; quadratic cost → hierarchical subsampling;
-   **Self-supervised learning**: geometric pretexts — predict descriptors (HKS: "know thyself"), local orientation, reconstruct masked regions; contrastive pre-training between views/poses of the same shape (the spirit of methods like SurfContrast): LLM pre-training applied to surfaces;
-   **Benchmarks**:
      Dataset          Task                                   Metric
      ---------------- -------------------------------------- ----------------------------
      FAUST / SCAPE    human correspondence (various poses)   mean geodesic error (×100)
      SHREC            shape retrieval                        mAP
      ModelNet40       cloud classification                   accuracy
      ShapeNet-parts   part segmentation                      mIoU

```python
# Mesh classification via LBO-features + small classifier (lab skeleton)
import torch
# features: [Gauss_curvature, Mean_curvature, HKS(t1..t5)] per vertex
model = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(7, 128), torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Linear(128, 64),
)
# invariant pooling: max over vertices, then classification head
pooled = model(features).max(dim=0).values.unsqueeze(0)   # (n, 64) -> max over vertices -> (1, 64)
# a linear head then maps (1, 64) -> (1, n_classes)

# DiffusionNet "learned diffusion" layer (truncated version):
m = 4                                                     # number of learned scales
t_params = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.rand(m))              # learned scales
def diffusion(H, evals, evecs, mass):                     # mass: lumped diagonal of M, shape (n,)
    H_spec = evecs.T @ (mass.unsqueeze(1) * H)            # M-weighted projection, (k, d)
    out = [H]
    for t in torch.nn.functional.softplus(t_params):
        out.append(evecs @ (torch.exp(-t * evals).unsqueeze(1) * H_spec))
    return torch.cat(out, dim=1)                          # concat of scales
```

## 7. Euclidean equivariance {#ch7}

A rotated or translated molecule is the same molecule, and a network should not have to learn this from data. This chapter defines equivariance, recalls why the EGNN layer respects the symmetries of Euclidean space by construction, and compares the invariant and equivariant networks used for molecules: SchNet, DimeNet and MACE.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Equivariance and invariance]{.tag} For a group $G$ acting on inputs and outputs: $f$ is *equivariant* if $$f(g \cdot x) = g \cdot f(x) \qquad \forall g \in G,$$ and *invariant* if $f(g\cdot x) = f(x)$. For clouds/meshes, the natural group is $E(n)$ (rotations $R$, translations $t$, reflections): a rotated molecule remains the same molecule — the network should neither relearn every orientation, nor confuse them.
:::

::: thm
[EGNN (Satorras, Hoogeboom, Welling — ICML 2021): equations]{.tag} State: positions $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$, features $h_i$. Layer:
$$m_{ij} = \phi_e\big(\|x_i - x_j\|^2,\ \|h_i - h_j\|^2,\ h_i, h_j\big) \qquad \text{(message, functions of distances only)}$$
$$x_i' = x_i + \sum_{j \ne i} (x_i - x_j)\,\phi_x(m_{ij}) \qquad \text{(equivariant update)}$$
$$h_i' = \phi_h\big(h_i, \textstyle\sum_j m_{ij}\big) \qquad \text{(invariant update)}.$$
:::

::: recap
[Recap — EGNN equivariance (Graph ML Proposition 8.3)]{.tag} The proof is that of [Graph ML, Proposition 8.3](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch8); these notes do not repeat it.

Under $x \mapsto Rx + t$ with $R$ orthogonal, every distance $\|x_i - x_j\|$ is unchanged, so every message $m_{ij}$ and every new feature $h_i'$ is invariant.

In the position update, the translation cancels in the differences $x_i - x_j$ and $R$ factors out of the sum, so the new positions transform as $x_i' \mapsto Rx_i' + t$.

By induction over the layers the network is $E(n)$-equivariant, and a sum of the $h_i$ gives an invariant readout. Exercise 5 asks you to write these steps out.
:::

::: thm
[Proposition 7.2 — An invariant energy gives equivariant forces]{.tag} Let $U(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ be the energy of a configuration of $n$ atoms, invariant under $E(3)$:
$$U(Rx_1 + t, \dots, Rx_n + t) = U(x_1, \dots, x_n) \qquad \text{for every orthogonal } R \text{ and every } t \in \mathbb{R}^3 .$$
Then the forces $F_i = -\nabla_{x_i} U$ are equivariant: they rotate with the molecule and ignore translations,
$$F_i(Rx_1 + t, \dots, Rx_n + t) = R\,F_i(x_1, \dots, x_n).$$
:::

::: proof
Differentiate the invariance identity with respect to $x_i$. By the chain rule, the left-hand side gives $R^\top (\nabla_{x_i} U)(Rx + t)$, evaluated at the moved configuration, and the right-hand side gives $(\nabla_{x_i} U)(x)$. Multiply both sides by $R$, use $RR^\top = I$ and change the sign. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Invariant or equivariant outputs? The target decides]{.tag}

-   **Scalars** (energy, HOMO–LUMO gap, solubility) are invariant: an invariant model suffices.
-   **Vectors** (forces, dipole moment) rotate with the molecule. Either predict an invariant energy and differentiate it — by Proposition 7.2 the forces are then exactly equivariant, and conservative — or output vectors from an equivariant channel, such as the coordinates of EGNN.
-   **Tensors** (the polarizability $\alpha$, which transforms as $R\,\alpha\,R^\top$) need hidden features of higher order: the MACE family below.
-   **Positions** (denoising in a diffusion model, conformer generation) need an equivariant output; the equivariant diffusion models met in [Graph Generative Models ch. 5](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html#ch5) (M2 P2) use EGNN-type layers for this.
-   **Mirror images.** Distances and angles do not change under a reflection ($\det R = -1$), so a model built on them alone cannot tell a molecule from its mirror image, although two mirror-image molecules (enantiomers) can act very differently as drugs. A chirality-aware model adds a quantity that changes sign under reflection, such as the signed volume of four atoms,
    $$\mathrm{vol}(i, j, k, l) = (x_j - x_i)\cdot\big[(x_k - x_i)\times(x_l - x_i)\big].$$
:::

::: def
[Three molecular networks: SchNet, DimeNet, MACE]{.tag} All three pass messages between the atoms that lie within a cutoff radius $c$ of each other; they differ in the geometry they read and in the features they carry. Write $d_{ij} = \|x_i - x_j\|$.

-   **SchNet** (Schütt et al., 2017) reads distances only. Its *continuous-filter convolution* weights each neighbour by a filter computed from the distance (simplified form):
    $$h_i \leftarrow h_i + \sum_{j \neq i,\ d_{ij} < c} h_j \odot W\big(e(d_{ij})\big), \qquad e_k(d) = \exp\big(-\gamma\,(d - \mu_k)^2\big),$$
    where $e$ expands the distance on Gaussians centred at $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K$ and $W$ is an MLP. The energy is a sum of atomic terms, and forces follow from Proposition 7.2.
-   **DimeNet** (Gasteiger, Groß & Günnemann, 2020) puts the messages $m_{ji}$ on directed edges and updates them with the angle $\alpha_{kji}$ between the bonds $k \to j$ and $j \to i$:
    $$m_{ji} \leftarrow f_{\mathrm{upd}}\Big(m_{ji},\ \sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(j) \setminus \{i\}} f_{\mathrm{int}}\big(m_{kj},\ d_{ji},\ d_{kj},\ \alpha_{kji}\big)\Big).$$
    Distances and angles are invariant, so the model stays invariant; the angles separate shapes that the distances to the neighbours confuse, at the cost of one term per pair of adjacent bonds.
-   **MACE** (Batatia et al., 2022) is equivariant. Each atom carries features $h_i^{(l)}$ of orders $l = 0, 1, \dots, L$ (scalars, vectors, higher tensors), which rotate with the Wigner matrices: $h_i^{(l)} \mapsto D^{(l)}(R)\,h_i^{(l)}$. A message combines a learned radial function of $d_{ij}$ with spherical harmonics of the direction from $i$ to $j$; tensor products of these messages build terms that involve up to four atoms in a single layer, and two layers give accurate force fields.
:::

**Why go beyond distances?** Around one atom, the multiset of distances to its neighbours does not determine its environment, and even the distances together with the angles can coincide for two different environments (Pozdnyakov et al., 2020). Angles (DimeNet) and higher body orders (MACE) shrink this blind spot, at a higher cost per layer.

| Model | Geometry read | Hidden features | Natural outputs | Cost per layer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EGNN | distances | scalars, plus updated coordinates | invariant scalars; equivariant positions | linear in the edges |
| SchNet | distances | scalars | invariant scalars; forces as $-\nabla U$ | linear in the edges |
| DimeNet | distances and angles | scalars on directed edges | invariant scalars; forces as $-\nabla U$ | one term per pair of adjacent bonds |
| MACE | distances and directions | features of orders $l \le L$ | scalars, vectors, tensors | grows with $L$ and with the body order |

-   **SE(3)-transformers (sketch)**: for the continuous version, attention is built on *equivariant fields* (irreducible representations; invariant keys/queries, vector-valued values) — the machinery exceeds this course, but the principle stands: invariant similarities, transformed values;
-   **Connections**: EGNN is a GNN whose messages are constrained by geometry — "geometry first, network second" — and the announced M2 P1 module Advanced GNN places it among its bridges (ch. 8); the molecule and protein applications are in ch. 8 below; conformer generation by equivariant diffusion (positions as an equivariant output) meets the diffusion models of Multimodal GenAI (ch. 3) and Graph Generative Models (ch. 5).

## 8. Applications and LLGA connections {#ch8}

This chapter gathers where the tools of the module are used — molecules, proteins, industry, shape generation — and how they connect to the graph, optimal transport and LLM tracks of the master.

-   **3D molecules**: a molecule is an equivariant cloud (EGNN, ch. 7) — conformer prediction (equilibrium geometries minimize energy; generation by equivariant diffusion meets the Multimodal GenAI module, ch. 3); properties (solvability, toxicity) via geometric descriptors (molecular HKS/WKS);
-   **Proteins**: binding interfaces = correspondence of *molecular surfaces* (shape complementarity — partial functional maps); docking; geometry meets the master's molecule-graph pipeline (Graph ML); worked example: binding-site segmentation, Example 8.1 below;
-   **Industry**: CAD/mesh retrieval, 3D scanning (reverse engineering: Poisson reconstruction of ch. 5), quality control by comparison to tolerances, dental/orthopedics (crowns = quasi-isometric shapes); autonomous vehicles (lidars = clouds → PointNet++/DGCNN); AR/VR: avatars (human body correspondence — FAUST in production), mesh compression (spectral coordinates);
-   **Shape generation**: diffusion on point clouds and meshes (noising/denoising positions and connectivities — exactly the DDPM of the Multimodal GenAI module, ch. 3, in $\mathbb{R}^{3n}$ with equivariance); the "shape-GPT" future: surface tokens;
-   **Connection 1 — graphs**: a mesh is a graph; the operators (Laplacian, diffusion, eigendecomposition) are shared with Graph ML/Advanced GNN;
-   **Connection 2 — OT**: shape correspondence ≈ transport; Gromov-Wasserstein compares intrinsic metrics (OT ch. 5);
-   **Connection 3 — LLM**: multimodal LLMs are starting to "see" objects; 3D tokens (surface patches) join image tokens; a "shape-GPT" that generates geometry? — a cross-cutting project topic.

::: ex
[Example 8.1 — Protein binding sites on a molecular surface (MaSIF-style)]{.tag} **Task.** Given one protein chain from the Protein Data Bank, predict which points of its surface touch a partner protein in a complex: a binary segmentation of the vertices, the "site" task of MaSIF (Gainza et al., *Nature Methods* 2020). Interfaces matter for drug design, because many therapeutic antibodies and small binders work by blocking one.

1.  **Mesh.** Compute the solvent-excluded surface of the chain and triangulate it at a resolution of about 1 Å; a chain of a few hundred residues gives a mesh of the order of 10,000 vertices.
2.  **Features per vertex.** Geometric: the HKS at a dozen log-spaced times (ch. 3), the mean curvature from $L\mathbf{x}$ (ch. 1) and the shape index. Chemical: the hydropathy of the closest residue, the electrostatic potential from a Poisson–Boltzmann solver and a hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor score. All are scalar fields on the surface, so none depends on the pose of the protein.
3.  **Network.** DiffusionNet (ch. 6) on the operators $(K, M)$ of the mesh. Its learned diffusion times set the size of the region each vertex looks at, and its gradient features tell concave pockets from convex bumps. MaSIF itself cut geodesic patches of fixed radius around each vertex; DiffusionNet needs no patches.
4.  **Labels and split.** A vertex is positive when the partner buries it in the complex. Split the training and test sets by protein, grouping similar sequences, never by vertex: neighbouring vertices of one protein are near-duplicates.
5.  **Metric.** ROC-AUC per protein, then the median over proteins. It needs no threshold and does not reward predicting "no interface" everywhere, although interfaces cover only a minority of the surface.

**AUC by hand.** Five vertices of a test protein, sorted by score: 0.9 (+), 0.8 (−), 0.7 (+), 0.4 (−), 0.2 (−). The AUC is the fraction of (positive, negative) pairs in the right order. The positive at 0.9 beats the three negatives and the one at 0.7 beats two of them, so
$$\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{3 + 2}{2 \times 3} = \frac56 \approx 0.83 .$$

**What can go wrong.** Training chains come from solved complexes, so their side chains are already in the bound conformation, which makes interfaces easier to spot than on a free protein: test on unbound structures when they exist. AtomSurf (Mallet, Attaiki, Miao, Correia and Ovsjanikov, 2024) compares surface encoders of the DiffusionNet family with graph encoders of the atoms, on binding-site identification among other tasks.
:::

## 9. Course research notes — Geometric Data Analysis (Ovsjanikov) {#ch9}

Maks Ovsjanikov heads the *Geometric Data Analysis* group at LIX (École Polytechnique). The four publications below are not merely "references" for this course: they *are* the course — every chapter from 2 to 6 stems directly from them.

::: thm
[Functional Maps — SIGGRAPH 2012 (the founding paper)]{.tag} M. Ovsjanikov, M. Ben-Chen, J. Solomon, A. Butscher, L. Guibas, [arXiv:1204.3967](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.3967) — Best Paper Award.

**The story.** Before 2012, shape correspondence was handled *point to point*: combinatorial matching of tens of thousands of vertices, fragile heuristics. The idea: represent the map as a *linear operator on functions* (ch. 4), which becomes a small matrix in spectral bases.

**Beyond chapter 4.** The paper also introduces: the effective computation of the constraints, the inverse conversion (matrix → correspondence), and above all the demonstration that *a few well-chosen constraints* suffice (descriptors + commutation).

**Extensions (by the hundreds)**: dense coupling, partial maps, the *shape Differences* formulation (comparing how two shapes transport functions), and the ZoomOut refinement below.

**Positioning.** It is one of the most influential papers of modern shape analysis; the framework is today the standard *and* the basis of learned methods (GeomFMaps).
:::

::: thm
[HKS — Sun, Ovsjanikov, Guibas, SGP 2009]{.tag} [A Concise and Provably Informative Multi-Scale Signature](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01515.x).

**The genesis.** The heat kernel $h_t(x, y)$ (ch. 2) transports information between points; its *diagonal* $h_t(x,x)$ — the heat that returns to its starting point — is a descriptor of $x$ at every scale $t$.

**Contributions.**

1.  the multi-scale characterization (small $t$ = local, large = global);
2.  the proof of isometric invariance *and* stability (the proved sketch of ch. 3);
3.  the analysis of the space of scales.

**Impact.** The HKS and its WKS variant are the input descriptors of almost all correspondence pipelines (including functional maps); the scale-invariant version extends it to heterogeneous scans.
:::

::: thm
[ZoomOut — SIGGRAPH Asia 2019]{.tag} S. Melzi, J. Ren, E. Rodolà, A. Sharma, P. Wonka, M. Ovsjanikov, [arXiv:1904.07865](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07865).

**Problem.** The spectrum truncated to $k$ eigenfunctions is a trade-off: small $k$ = robust but coarse; large $k$ = precise but noisy.

**Idea.** The iterative spectral refinement of ch. 4: reconstruct a *hard* correspondence at resolution $k$, reinject it as a coupling constraint at resolution $k + \Delta$, and repeat. The regularization emerges from the upsampling rhythm; no additional data is required.

**Results.** Substantial improvements on mediocre initial correspondences, near-zero cost (matrix products); it became the standard post-processor.

**Positioning.** The "soft ↔ hard" loop is the geometric ancestor of iterative refinements; its spirit resurfaces in the local/global solvers of ch. 5.
:::

::: thm
[DiffusionNet — TOG 2022]{.tag} N. Sharp, S. Attaiki, K. Crane, M. Ovsjanikov, [arXiv:2012.00888](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00888).

**Problem.** All "CNN-like" architectures on surfaces depend on the discretization (mesh vs cloud, resolution) and run into the gauge problem (ch. 6).

**Idea.** A minimal and geometrically honest layer: diffusion at *learned* scales + pointwise MLP + feature gradient — complete equations in ch. 6.

**Results.** SOTA correspondence (FAUST, SCAPE, SHREC'07 non-rigid), demonstrated robustness to discretization changes, works on clouds without a mesh (diffusion is replayed via Monte-Carlo estimation of heat).

**Positioning.** The prototype of "sober geometric deep learning": instead of adapting convolution to the surface, inject the physical *operator* (heat) as a learning building block — the convergence of chapters 2 (operators) and 6 (networks).
:::

::: note
[The common thread]{.tag} HKS (2009: eigenfunctions as descriptors) → Functional Maps (2012: the map as an operator) → ZoomOut (2019: spectral refinement) → DiffusionNet (2022: the operator inside the network): fifteen years of research that follow exactly the progression of this course — from the spectral to deep learning.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Cotangents.** Verify that the cotangent matrix is symmetric and that $L\mathbf{1} = 0$; check on a flat mesh (the Laplacian must vanish at interior points).
2.  **★ Gauss–Bonnet on the cube.** Verify numerically theorem 1.3 on the cube meshed into 12 triangles; what happens to the sum of deficits if each face is subdivided into 4? (answer: unchanged — why?).
3.  **★ Spectrum = fingerprint.** Compute the first 20 eigenvalues of $\Delta$ for two rigid shapes and their articulated (bent) versions; plot the superimposed spectra and comment on the isometric invariance.
4.  **★ Heat kernel and PDEs.** Verify that $h_t(x, y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y)$ solves $\partial_t h_t = \Delta_y h_t$, $h_0(x, y) = \delta_x(y)$, and deduce that $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0$ diffuses any initial condition.
5.  **★ EGNN invariance.** In the equations of ch. 7, show that the messages $m_{ij}$ depend only on distances that are mutually invariant under $E(n)$, and that the position update remains equivariant.
6.  **★★ Stiffness of a triangle.** On a triangle $T = (i, j, k)$ with hat functions $\psi_i, \psi_j, \psi_k$, show that
    $$\int_T \langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle\, dA = -\frac12\cot\theta_k,$$
    where $\theta_k$ is the angle at vertex $k$, opposite to edge $(i,j)$.
7.  **★★ HKS.** Show that $\mathrm{HKS}(x, t)$ is isometrically invariant; compute and visualize multi-scale HKS on a FAUST human — identify the "self-descriptive points" (hands, head).
8.  **★★ Toy functional map.** Two known isometric meshes: build $C$ by least squares (descriptor + commutation constraints); reconstruct the correspondence; measure the mean geodesic error; what happens if $k$ is too small?
9.  **★★ Spectral commutation.** Show that if $T : M \to N$ is an isometry, then $T_F \Delta_M = \Delta_N T_F$, and that in the eigenbasis this forces $C\Lambda_M \approx \Lambda_N C$ — hence the structure (almost block-diagonal over clusters of close eigenvalues) of $C$.
10. **★★ PointNet invariance.** Show that max pooling *and* the product are permutation-invariant, but that the product is numerically unstable (explosion/underflow of multiplicative gradients) while the mean dilutes local signals; implement the three aggregators and check on a permuted cloud (stability + selectivity of a discriminative sub-region).
11. **★★★ DiffusionNet vs GCN.** On FAUST (correspondence): compare a GCN on the graph of the mesh vs DiffusionNet (learned scales); discuss why diffusion is a good geometric "mixer".
12. **★★★ Project.** Shape retrieval: extract (HKS, spectrum, curvatures) → aggregation → similarity by optimal transport ($W_1$ on descriptor distributions); evaluate the mAP on a subset of SHREC; the three connections of the course at work.

::: note
[Solution 1 — Symmetry and constants]{.tag} Each edge weight $w_{ij} = \frac12(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij})$ is constructed symmetrically in $i, j$ (the two opposite angles favor neither endpoint): $W = W^\top$.

And $L\mathbf{1} = 0$ because the diagonal term of each row $i$ is the opposite of the sum of the off-diagonal weights:
$$-\sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij} + \sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij} = 0 .$$

On a regular flat grid, the contributions of the neighbors cancel out and $Lf = 0$ at interior points; at the boundary, the angle deficit gives a nonzero Laplacian — that is the boundary!
:::

::: note
[Solution 2 — Gauss–Bonnet on the cube]{.tag} Each corner receives three angles of $\pi/2$:
$$\text{deficit } 2\pi - 3\times\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \text{total } 8\times\frac{\pi}{2} = 4\pi = 2\pi\chi \text{ with } \chi = 2.$$
The vertices added by subdivision (face centers, edge midpoints) are flat — zero deficit — and the 8 corners keep their $\frac{\pi}{2}$: the sum is *unchanged*.

This illustrates that the right-hand side of Gauss–Bonnet is topological; it is a practical integrity test for a closed mesh: $\sum_iK_iA_i = 2\pi\chi$ whatever the resolution.
:::

::: note
[Solution 4 — The heat kernel solves the PDE]{.tag} Term-by-term derivative:
$$\partial_t h_t(x,y) = -\sum_k\lambda_ke^{-\lambda_kt}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y),$$
and $\Delta_yh_t(x,y)$ gives the same sum after applying $\Delta\phi_k = -\lambda_k\phi_k$ to the second factor — equal.

As $t \to 0$, $h_t(x,\cdot) \to \delta_x$ (an approximate identity family, orthonormal basis); by superposition, $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0$ with each mode damped by $e^{-\lambda_kt}$.
:::

::: note
[Solution 6 — Stiffness of a triangle]{.tag} **Case $i \ne j$**: redo step 2 of derivation 2.2. $\nabla\psi_i$ is constant, orthogonal to the opposite side, with norm $1/h_i$; the angle between $\nabla\psi_i$ and $\nabla\psi_j$ equals $\pi - \theta_k$, hence
$$\int_T\langle\nabla\psi_i,\nabla\psi_j\rangle dA = |T|\cdot\big(-\frac{\cos\theta_k}{h_ih_j}\big) = -\frac12\cot\theta_k$$
(via $h_i = 2|T|/|e_{jk}|$, $h_j = 2|T|/|e_{ik}|$, $|T| = \frac12|e_{jk}||e_{ik}|\sin\theta_k$).

**Case $i = j$**:
$$\int_T\|\nabla\psi_i\|^2 dA = |T|/h_i^2 = \frac{|e_{jk}|}{2h_i} = \frac12(\cot\theta_j + \cot\theta_k),$$
because the height from $i$ splits the opposite side into segments $h_i\cot\theta_j$ and $h_i\cot\theta_k$ (an algebraic identity, also valid for obtuse angles via the signs of the cotangents).
:::

::: note
[Solution 7 — HKS invariance]{.tag} By theorem 2.5 (proved invariance), $\phi_k^N \circ T$ is an eigenfunction of $M$ for $\lambda_k^N$. The spectra coincide after sorting and, if the eigenvalues are simple, $\phi_k^N(Tx) = \pm\phi_k^M(x)$. Then
$$\mathrm{HKS}_N(Tx,t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_kt}\phi_k^N(Tx)^2 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_kt}\phi_k^M(x)^2 = \mathrm{HKS}_M(x,t)$$
(the square kills the sign; for multiple eigenvalues: equality after a basis rotation within each eigenspace).

On FAUST: at small $t$, extremities (hands, head) = self-descriptive points; at large $t$, convergence toward the constant component — hence the logarithmic grid in $t$.
:::

::: note
[Solution 9 — Commutation and the structure of C]{.tag} The proof of 4.2 establishes
$$T_F\phi_k^N = \pm\phi_{\sigma(k)}^M \quad\text{with}\quad \lambda_k^N = \lambda_{\sigma(k)}^M .$$
The matrix of $T_F$ in eigenbases is therefore block-diagonal — $C_{ij} \ne 0$ only if $\lambda_i^M$ and $\lambda_j^N$ coincide.

For quasi-isometric surfaces, the equalities become proximities: the soft constraint $\|C\Lambda_M - \Lambda_NC\|_F^2$ encodes this structure, locks the frequency correspondences, and blocks spectrally absurd matchings. Limitation: close or multiple eigenvalues leave undecided blocks — resolved by the descriptor constraints.
:::

::: note
[Solution 10 — PointNet aggregators]{.tag} Max and product are permutation-invariant (reordering a set changes neither its max nor its product); experiment confirms this on a permuted cloud. But:

a.  the product of $n$ factors below 1 collapses (underflow) and multiplies the gradients — unstable;
b.  the mean is stable but dilutes: if 1% of the cloud carries the discriminative signal, it drowns it where the max captures it;
c.  the max learns local "detectors" — the building block of universality (proof of 6.1).
:::
